document.title: Afghan Supplemental (Kabul 000509)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
document.note: [Secret] Neumann warns that minimizing economic assistance and leaving out infrastructure 'plays into the Taliban strategy.' He pleads for more money and a shift in priorities. A resurgent Taliban says 'You have all the clocks but we have all the time.'

organizations.name: Taliban
organizations.notes: A Taliban leader (name redacted) is quoted as saying 'you have all the clocks but we have all the time.' The Ambassador argues that cutting infrastructure funding plays into the Taliban strategy and message that time is on their side.

organizations.name: U.S. Embassy Kabul
organizations.notes: Originator of the cable under Ambassador Ronald E. Neumann. It argues for supplemental funding for roads, power and agriculture.

organizations.name: U.S. Department of State
organizations.notes: Recipient of the cable, which is addressed to 'Madame Secretary' (the Secretary of State, not named in the text).

organizations.name: Office of Management and Budget
organizations.notes: Named in the subject line ('AFGHAN SUPPLEMENTAL-OMB RULES'). The OMB rules constrain the supplemental funding request.

organizations.name: Government of Afghanistan
organizations.notes: The Ambassador says that without power and business the GOA cannot tax, and that funding shortfalls will slow the building of Afghan government outside Kabul.

organizations.name: Provincial Reconstruction Teams
organizations.notes: Cited in connection with reduced quick impact funding.

organizations.name: U.S. Congress
organizations.notes: The cable says every member who has visited Kabul left persuaded of the need for infrastructure supplemental funding.

events.description: Ambassador Neumann sends an immediate-precedence cable to the Secretary of State objecting to the plan to minimize economic and infrastructure assistance in the Afghan supplemental, citing roads, energy and agriculture needs and the Taliban's time-is-on-our-side narrative.
The Embassy recommended more roads, power and agriculture assistance for the FY07 budget; the FY05 supplemental also only began to reach the Embassy in September.

Ambassador Ronald Neumann sends a cable to Secretary of State urging infrastructure funding (roads, power, agriculture) in the Afghan supplemental, warning the Taliban message that time is on their side will resonate.
The Ambassador made a recommendation for more roads, power, and agriculture assistance for the '07 budget.
The FY05 supplemental funds began to reach the Embassy in Kabul.

relationships.detail: The Taliban strategy of waiting out the US is contrasted with the US offensive in governance and development proposed by the Ambassador.
relationships.quote: The supplemental decision recommendation to minimize economic assistance and leave out infrastructure plays to the Taliban strategy, not to ours.

relationships.detail: Reduced funding would make the Taliban's role easier and slow the building of the Afghan government outside Kabul.
relationships.quote: It will make it slower to build the Afghan government outside Kabul. It will make the margin of our victory tighter and the Taliban's role easier.

relationships.detail: OMB rules on the supplemental restricted the embassy's requested infrastructure funding; the Ambassador objects (subject line AFGHAN SUPPLEMENTAL-OMB RULES).
Members of Congress visiting Kabul left persuaded of the need for infrastructure supplemental funding.
relationships.quote: Every member of Congress who has visited Kabul has left persuaded of the need for supplemental funding for infrastructure.

sources_cited: U.S. Embassy Kabul cable 06KABUL509 (Afghan Supplemental-OMB Rules), declassified by the State Department
key_claims: The Ambassador argues that minimizing economic aid and excluding infrastructure from the supplemental plays to the Taliban strategy of outlasting the coalition.
He cites a Taliban leader's remark: 'you have all the clocks but we have all the time.'
He warns that lacking roads, power and agriculture funding will raise opium poppy production and make the Taliban message that time is on their side resonate.
He says roughly USD 400 million in missing funds will not lose the war but will make the narcotics problem worse and slow Afghan government-building outside Kabul.
He asks that infrastructure be treated as part of a war effort not bound by all peacetime budget rules.
